front_blocks.md: Define **electromagnetic induction**.

back_blocks.md: **Electromagnetic induction** (the **generator effect**) is when a **potential difference** is induced in a conductor or coil as it moves through a magnetic field, or as the magnetic field through it changes. If the conductor is part of a complete circuit, a **current** is also induced.

cards.front_md: Define **electromagnetic induction**.

If the conductor is part of a complete circuit, a **current** is also induced.

front_blocks.md: Define the **motor effect**.

back_blocks.md: The **motor effect** is when a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a **force**. It is the opposite of the generator effect, in which movement induces a current rather than a current producing movement.

cards.front_md: Define the **motor effect**.
cards.back_md: The **motor effect** is when a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a **force**. It is the opposite of the generator effect, in which movement induces a current rather than a current producing movement.

front_blocks.md: What condition must be met for a potential difference to be induced in a conductor?

back_blocks.md: There must be **relative movement** between the conductor and the magnetic field, so that the conductor **cuts through** the magnetic field lines.

cards.front_md: What condition must be met for a potential difference to be induced in a conductor?
cards.back_md: There must be **relative movement** between the conductor and the magnetic field, so that the conductor **cuts through** the magnetic field lines.

front_blocks.md: State four factors that affect the size of the potential difference induced in a coil.

back_blocks.md: **Speed** of movement of the wire, coil or magnet; **number of turns** on the coil; **size (area)** of the coil; **strength** of the magnetic field. Increasing any of these increases the induced potential difference.

front_blocks.md: What piece of equipment can be used to measure the size of an induced potential difference?

back_blocks.md: A **sensitive voltmeter**.

front_blocks.md: Increasing the **______** of the magnetic field increases the size of the induced potential difference.

back_blocks.md: Increasing the **strength** of the magnetic field increases the size of the induced potential difference.

cards.front_md: Increasing the **______** of the magnetic field increases the size of the induced potential difference.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Reversing the direction in which a magnet is moved through a coil has no effect on the induced potential difference.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Reversing the direction of movement reverses the **direction** of the induced potential difference — the direction depends on the orientation of the magnet's poles and the direction of movement.

front_blocks.md: Define **alternator**.

back_blocks.md: An **alternator** is a generator that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy as **alternating current**. It consists of a rotating coil in a magnetic field, connected to the circuit by **slip rings** and brushes.

cards.front_md: Define **alternator**.
cards.back_md: An **alternator** is a generator that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy as **alternating current**. It consists of a rotating coil in a magnetic field, connected to the circuit by **slip rings** and brushes.

front_blocks.md: Define **dynamo**.

back_blocks.md: A **dynamo** is a **direct current** generator. It is built the same way as an alternator, except it uses a **split-ring commutator** instead of slip rings.

cards.front_md: Define **dynamo**.
cards.back_md: A **dynamo** is a **direct current** generator. It is built the same way as an alternator, except it uses a **split-ring commutator** instead of slip rings.

front_blocks.md: Why does an alternator produce an alternating current?

back_blocks.md: The rotating coil **cuts through** the magnetic field lines, and the slip rings maintain the same connection to the coil throughout rotation, so the induced potential difference (and current) repeatedly **reverses direction** as the coil turns.

cards.front_md: Why does an alternator produce an alternating current?
cards.back_md: The rotating coil **cuts through** the magnetic field lines, and the slip rings maintain the same connection to the coil throughout rotation, so the induced potential difference (and current) repeatedly **reverses direction** as the coil turns.

front_blocks.md: How does a split-ring commutator keep a dynamo's output current flowing in one direction?

back_blocks.md: The split-ring commutator swaps the connections between the coil and the brushes every half turn (each time the coil is perpendicular to the field), so the current leaving the dynamo stays **always positive** (or always negative), varying from zero to a maximum twice each cycle.

cards.front_md: How does a split-ring commutator keep a dynamo's output current flowing in one direction?

front_blocks.md: Besides rotating a coil within a magnetic field, how else can an alternating current be generated?

back_blocks.md: By rotating a **magnet** within a stationary coil. What matters is the **relative motion** between the coil and the magnet.

cards.front_md: Besides rotating a coil within a magnetic field, how else can an alternating current be generated?

front_blocks.md: A dynamo produces **______** current, while an alternator produces **______** current.

back_blocks.md: A dynamo produces **direct** current, while an alternator produces **alternating** current.

cards.front_md: A dynamo produces **______** current, while an alternator produces **______** current.
cards.back_md: A dynamo produces **direct** current, while an alternator produces **alternating** current.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The current output from a dynamo periodically reverses polarity, in the same way as an alternator's output.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

A dynamo's output current never reverses polarity — it varies between zero and a maximum twice per cycle but stays always positive (or always negative), unlike an alternator's output, which alternates between positive and negative.

front_blocks.md: Define **transformer**.

back_blocks.md: A **transformer** is a device that uses the generator effect to change the value of an alternating potential difference or current. It consists of a **primary coil**, a **secondary coil**, and an **iron core**.

cards.front_md: Define **transformer**.
cards.back_md: A **transformer** is a device that uses the generator effect to change the value of an alternating potential difference or current. It consists of a **primary coil**, a **secondary coil**, and an **iron core**.

front_blocks.md: Define **step-up transformer**.

back_blocks.md: A **step-up transformer** increases the potential difference of a power source. It has **more turns** on the secondary coil than on the primary coil.

cards.front_md: Define **step-up transformer**.
cards.back_md: A **step-up transformer** increases the potential difference of a power source. It has **more turns** on the secondary coil than on the primary coil.

front_blocks.md: Define **step-down transformer**.

back_blocks.md: A **step-down transformer** decreases the potential difference of a power source. It has **fewer turns** on the secondary coil than on the primary coil.

cards.front_md: Define **step-down transformer**.
cards.back_md: A **step-down transformer** decreases the potential difference of a power source. It has **fewer turns** on the secondary coil than on the primary coil.

front_blocks.md: Why is iron used for the core of a transformer?

back_blocks.md: **Iron** is easily **magnetised**, so the changing magnetic field produced by the primary coil passes through the core efficiently and reaches the secondary coil.

cards.front_md: Why is iron used for the core of a transformer?
cards.back_md: **Iron** is easily **magnetised**, so the changing magnetic field produced by the primary coil passes through the core efficiently and reaches the secondary coil.

front_blocks.md: Explain how an alternating potential difference in the primary coil induces a potential difference in the secondary coil.

back_blocks.md: The alternating current in the primary coil produces a **changing magnetic field**. The iron core carries this changing field to the secondary coil, where it **cuts through** the turns and **induces** an alternating potential difference with the **same frequency** as the primary supply.

cards.front_md: Explain how an alternating potential difference in the primary coil induces a potential difference in the secondary coil.
cards.back_md: The alternating current in the primary coil produces a **changing magnetic field**. The iron core carries this changing field to the secondary coil, where it **cuts through** the turns and **induces** an alternating potential difference with the **same frequency** as the primary supply.

front_blocks.md: Why is electricity transmitted at high voltage using step-up transformers in the national grid?

back_blocks.md: For the same power, a higher voltage means a **lower current**, and a lower current reduces the **energy lost as heat** in the transmission cables.

cards.front_md: Why is electricity transmitted at high voltage using step-up transformers in the national grid?

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A transformer works when connected to a constant direct current supply.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
A transformer only works with an **alternating current** supply. A constant direct current produces a magnetic field that does not change, so no potential difference is induced in the secondary coil.

front_blocks.md: Define an **ideal transformer**.

back_blocks.md: An **ideal transformer** is 100% efficient, so the **input power** equals the **output power**:
$V_{p} \times I_{p} = V_{s} \times I_{s}$

front_blocks.md: A transformer has 20 turns on its primary coil and 800 turns on its secondary coil. The primary potential difference is 500 V. Calculate the secondary potential difference.

back_blocks.md: $V_{s} = \frac{n_{s}}{n_{p}} \times V_{p} = \frac{800}{20} \times 500 = 20000 \text{V}$

front_blocks.md: A step-up transformer in a travel adapter steps 115 V up to 230 V to supply a hairdryer drawing 5 A. Assuming 100% efficiency, calculate the current drawn from the 115 V mains supply.

back_blocks.md: $I_{p} = \frac{V_{s}\timesI_{s}}{V_{p}} = \frac{230\times5}{115} = 10 \text{A}$

back_blocks.md: In the transformer equation, the ratio of the potential differences across the two coils is equal to the ratio of the number of **turns** on each coil.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
An ideal transformer that steps up the potential difference also increases the power delivered to the secondary circuit.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

By conservation of energy, an ideal transformer cannot increase power: input power equals output power ($V_{p} \times I_{p} = V_{s} \times I_{s}$), so an increase in potential difference is matched by a proportional decrease in current.
